html:
The first known book about tea, written by Lu Yu in Tang China between about 760 and 762. It covers where tea grows, how to pick and process it, the tools and water to use, how to brew and drink it, and its history.

Lu Yu was raised in a Buddhist monastery. During the An Lushan rebellion he settled in what is now Zhejiang, where he lived among poets and scholars. In his day tea was pressed into cakes, roasted, ground and boiled. He set out exact steps and treated the whole process as a discipline. For him, tea carried a sense of the harmony of the universe, an idea close to the Buddhist, Daoist and Confucian thought of his time. His original manuscript is lost; the oldest surviving editions date from the Ming.

Why it matters:

  • It turned tea drinking from a regional and medicinal habit into a refined art with its own rules.
  • It helped tea spread across China, and with Buddhist monks to Korea and Japan, where it shaped the later tea ceremony of Sen no Rikyu.
  • Tea became a major trade good. Centuries later, demand for it in Britain helped lead to the Opium War.

Lu Yu came to be honoured as the sage of tea.
